blocks.alt: Two streams of water shoot from nozzles on a stone fountain rim and fall back into the basin. Each stream makes a smooth downward-opening arc; the highest point of each arc is visible against a park fence and trees.

blocks.text: Look at the water leaving the fountain. Each stream goes up and comes down.

blocks.prompt: Choose one stream. Name the highest point of that stream, the place the water does not go above. Say where it is on the photograph. The photograph cannot be marked. Do not measure, and do not write an equation yet.

blocks.text: That turning point is the fact we will want from an equation of the curve. Vertex form makes the high or low point readable.
A quadratic written as

is in vertex form. The vertex is the point \((h, k)\). The axis of symmetry is the vertical line \(x = h\). The sign of \(a\) tells you whether that vertex is a maximum or a minimum: negative \(a\) opens downward, so the vertex is a highest point; positive \(a\) opens upward, so the vertex is a lowest point.
Consider \(f(x) = (x + 3)^2 + 1\). The equation is already in vertex form, but notice the sign inside the brackets.

blocks.prompt: Name the vertex and the axis of symmetry. Do not sketch yet.

blocks.text: In this course, \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\) is vertex form. The expanded equation \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) is standard form.
Read the turning point from the equation
You named a vertex from a plus inside the brackets. Read this next equation the same way: vertex, axis, and whether the turning point is a maximum or a minimum.
Consider
Name the vertex. Is the vertex a maximum or a minimum? How did you know?
Compare the equation with \(y = a(x - h)^2 + k\).
The brackets contain \((x + 2)\). Vertex form uses \((x - h)\), so rewrite \(x + 2\) as \(x - (-2)\). That makes \(h = -2\). The constant outside the brackets is \(+4\), so \(k = 4\).
The vertex is \((-2, 4)\). The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the vertex, \(x = -2\).

The coefficient in front of the brackets is \(-3\). Because \(a\) is negative, the parabola opens downward, so the vertex is a maximum. The maximum value of the function is \(4\), and it occurs when \(x = -2\).
That highest point is the same kind of fact you named on the water stream, now read from the equation.
A second equation, with nothing added outside
The last equation had a constant outside the brackets, so \(k\) was easy to see as a height. Consider
The brackets contain \((x + 1)\). Rewrite \(x + 1\) as \(x - (-1)\), so \(h = -1\). There is no constant added outside, so \(k = 0\). The vertex is \((-1, 0)\), and the axis is \(x = -1\).

The coefficient is \(-2\), so \(a\) is negative and the parabola opens downward. The vertex is a maximum even though \(k = 0\). Maximum versus minimum comes from the sign of \(a\), not from whether \(k\) looks positive.

blocks.prompt: Where is the vertex? Does this graph have a maximum or a minimum? Could you decide that from \(k\) alone?

blocks.label: Match the equation you already read

blocks.text: Do not move the graph yet. Keep the point you wrote. Then move the graph until it matches \(f(x) = (x + 3)^2 + 1\). Submit when the live equation labelled Vertex form, above the graph, matches that equation.

blocks.prompt: Compare the vertex marker with the point you named. What in the equation told you the vertex? What did you have to change to match this equation?

blocks.text: Someone else’s first step
You just matched \((x + 3)\) to vertex form. These next items ask you to locate an invalid first step, and to test a claim about the axis.
Change only the horizontal position
The graph is back at \(f(x) = 2(x + 3)^2 + 1\). Do not move the graph yet.

blocks.prompt: Start from \(f(x) = 2(x + 3)^2 + 1\). If only \(h\) changes so the vertex sits at \(x = 2\), what happens to the graph, and what is the new equation? Write that before you move a graph.

blocks.text: Then move the graph so the vertex is at \(x = 2\), changing only \(h\) if you can. Submit. Say which quantity you meant to change: \(a\), \(h\), or \(k\).

blocks.prompt: Look at the live equation labelled Vertex form, above the graph, and the dashed vertical line. What changed? What stayed the same? How do you read the new vertex from the equation?

blocks.text: The same curve, two forms
Vertex form makes the turning point easy to read. Expanding that form into \(ax^2 + bx + c\) should not move the curve.
Rewrite
in standard form, meaning \(g(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\). Then check two \(x\)-values in both forms.
Square the binomial: \((x + 2)^2 = x^2 + 4x + 4\).
Multiply by \(a = \frac{1}{2}\): \(\frac{1}{2}x^2 + 2x + 2\).
At \(x = -2\), both forms give \(-3\). At \(x = 0\), both give \(-1\). Those table points sit on the same graph: expanding did not make a new parabola.

Now expand the starting equation from the graph, \(f(x) = 2(x + 3)^2 + 1\). If you rewrite it as \(ax^2 + bx + c\), will the graph be a different parabola or the same one? Write that down before you expand.

blocks.label: Expand, then check the same graph

blocks.text: Expand on paper. Enter your \(b\) and \(c\) (\(a\) should stay 2), then submit. Do not copy an expanded line off the graph until after you have tried.

blocks.prompt: Do a few table points sit on both forms? If you plotted a second curve from your expanded coefficients, do the two graphs land on top of each other?

blocks.text: Expand a new equation yourself
Here, standard form means \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\). Expand the vertex form yourself first, then compare the graphs. Do not skip the expansion by only reading a line off the graph.
How you know two forms are the same
You expanded and checked a few table points. These next items ask which method proves the forms match for every \(x\), and they ask you to repair a first invalid expansion step.
What vertex form is for
Consider \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\). What can you read from vertex form that is harder to see when the same function is written in standard form \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\)? Do not rewrite the function.

From vertex form you can read the vertex \((h, k)\), the axis \(x = h\), and whether the vertex is a maximum or a minimum from the sign of \(a\). Standard form makes the \(y\)-intercept \(c\) easy to see. Zeros are not obvious in either of those two forms unless they happen to sit on an axis.

Factored form \(f(x) = a(x - r)(x - s)\) makes the \(x\)-intercepts easy to see. Vertex form does not make those intercepts as obvious, and the vertex is not an intercept unless it actually sits on an axis.
Zeros from vertex form
Intercepts are not readable from vertex form the way they are from factored form. You can still find zeros by undoing the operations in the equation.
Write an equation from stated facts

You have been reading \(a\), \(h\), and \(k\) from a given equation. These next items ask you to write a vertex-form equation from a vertex and another point, from a labelled graph, or from a turning point that does not fix \(a\).

If the graph is not available, work on paper with \(f(x) = 2(x + 3)^2 + 1\). First look at \(f(x) = (x + 3)^2 + 1\): name that vertex, then sketch both equations (same turning point, different stretch). From the starting equation, predict what happens if you change only \(h\) to 2; rewrite the equation and sketch again. Expand the starting equation yourself and check that a few table points still sit on the same sketch.

blocks.text: If you are on paper: sketch from the equation, then change one of \(a\), \(h\), or \(k\) and sketch again.
A high point from a given model
You just read a high point from an equation of a path like the stream. These next models are already in vertex form.
What vertex form gives you

Vertex form \(f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k\) makes the vertex \((h, k)\) and the axis \(x = h\) readable. Maximum versus minimum comes from the sign of \(a\), not from the sign of \(k\) and not from which quadrant the vertex sits in.
Match the brackets to \((x - h)\). A plus inside the brackets does not mean the vertex is on the positive side of the \(x\)-axis.
\(a\) stretches or flips the graph. \(k\) moves the vertex up or down. Those two jobs are not the same.
Expanding vertex form into \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) gives the same parabola, not a new one. The graphs should land on top of each other.
